Federal Rule 65 authorizes the federal court to issue a preliminary injunction, but does not set forth the standard for granting or
denying the request. The standard is judicially defined, and looks to four factors: the plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction “must
establish” that the party is “likely to succeed on the merits”; “likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary relief;” that
“the balance of equities tips” in the movant’s favor”; and that an injunction “is in the public interest.” WINTER v. NATURAL
RESOURCES DEFENSE COUNCIL, 555 U.S. 7, 20, 129 S.Ct. 365, 374, 172 L.Ed.2d 249, 261 (2008). The entry of a preliminary
injunction is regarded as “extraordinary” relief, and may be awarded only upon “a clear showing that the plaintiff is entitled to such
relief.” Id. at 376, 129 S.Ct. at 22, 172 L.Ed.2d at 262. In Winter environmental groups sued the United States Navy to stop sonar testing
that was alleged to be harmful to marine mammals living in waters near Southern California. The Supreme Court reversed the grant of the
preliminary injunction, in part because the appellate court had required plaintiffs to show a possibility, and not a likelihood, of irreparable
harm. In the wake of Winter, the appellate courts have divided on whether the test for a preliminary injunction permits a “sliding scale”
approach to the four factors, or whether each factor must be “satisfied as articulated.” Alliance for the Wild Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d
1127, 1131 (9th Cir. 2011).
b.Temporary Restraining Orders
Federal Rule 65 authorizes the federal courts to issue a temporary restraining order. Unlike the preliminary injunction, an application
for a restraining order is sought when time considerations do not provide the opportunity for formal notice. Thus, a “TRO” is appropriate
only when the threat of irreparable injury is immediate and the need to preserve the status quo is urgent. Because of a concern over the
potential unfairness of ex parte proceedings, a number of special conditions, such as those set out in Federal Rule 65(b), are usually
imposed. The factors considered in ruling on a motion for a TRO are the same as for a preliminary injunction, and courts tend to proceed

ex parte only when there is “no reasonable alternative.” American Can Co. v. Mansukhani, 742 F.2d 314, 322 (7th Cir. 1984). See 11A
Wright & Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure § 2951 (3d ed.).
TROs issued after adversary hearings or that exceed the expiration provisions set out in Rule 65(b) are evaluated as de facto
preliminary injunctions by courts. See SAMPSON v. MURRAY, 415 U.S. 61, 94 S.Ct. 937, 39 L.Ed.2d 166 (1974). In Commodity
